records.group_headline: Learning outcomes, content, competencies, values and PCIs now use the KICD March 2025 wording (the data had a longer, reworded list of nine outcomes and different competencies, values and PCIs); the extra links the lessons use are kept and labelled as additional.
records.why: The data listed nine reworded outcomes (a to i). KICD gives six, and the March 2025 wording is verbatim. Mapping: (a) centre and linear scale factor = Lessons 4 and 10; (b) construct the image = Lessons 8 and 9; (c) area and volume scale factor = Lessons 6 and 7; (d) relate the three factors = Lessons 7 and 11; (e) apply to real life = Lessons 5 and 11; (f) appreciate = every lesson's attitudes and Final Explanation Section 5(e). The old outcomes 'identify similar figures' and 'state the properties' are the KICD learning experience 'review the properties of similar figures' and are still taught in Lessons 2 and 3. Teachers decide whether to keep the extra competencies, value (Unity) and PCIs that the lessons already use; they are kept below the KICD text and labelled as additional.

records.value:
• A map of Kenya in an atlas and a large wall map of Kenya show Lake Victoria and Mombasa with the same shape, though the sizes differ greatly.
• A matchbox-size model of a matatu looks just like the real matatu, but its paint and material needs are very different.
• A tailor in Gikomba market cuts small and large versions of the same dress pattern; when every length is doubled the large version needs about four times as much cloth, not twice as much.
• A slide or overhead projector in a classroom enlarges a small picture into a large image on the wall; the lens turns the image upside down (so the slide is loaded upside down), yet the shape of the picture is kept.
records.group_headline: The projector 'flip' was explained wrongly and the torch-and-cut-out demonstration could not show an inverted image; now a pinhole demonstration (which does invert) and correct wording.
records.why: Two supporting phenomena were scientifically loose. (1) A projector lens inverts the image, so the slide is loaded upside down; it is not 'flipped when the lens is reversed'. (2) Doubling every length of a pattern multiplies the cloth area by 2 x 2 = 4 (checked: 2 squared = 4), so 'much more than twice' is now stated as about four times. Lesson 9's torch-and-cut-out demonstration makes an upright shadow, not an inverted image, so it is replaced by a pinhole demonstration (next records).
records.reference: Eugene Hecht, Optics (Pearson), sections on the pinhole camera and image formation in lenses; Euclid's Elements Book VI on similar figures

records.old: Part B: a short projector demonstration: Mrs Achieng holds a cut-out triangle in front of a torch (or a pinhole in a card on a sunny wall) and learners see the inverted, enlarged image on the wall.
records.new: Part B: a short teacher-led pinhole demonstration (about 3 minutes): in a dimmed room Mrs Achieng holds a card with a small pinhole between a bright shape (a torch shining through an arrow or letter F cut from card, or a bright window) and a white sheet used as a screen, and learners see an upside-down image of the bright shape on the sheet. The pinhole plays the part of the centre O: the image is on the opposite side of O, like a negative scale factor. Moving the screen farther from the pinhole makes the image larger, and moving it closer makes it smaller.
records.why: A torch behind a cut-out casts an upright shadow, so it cannot show an inverted image. A pinhole forms an inverted image; its size ratio equals screen distance divided by object distance, which matches |k| for a centre of enlargement with negative k. Checked with similar triangles through the pinhole.
records.reference: Eugene Hecht, Optics (Pearson), section on the pinhole camera

records.old: For the projector demonstration, stand to the side, switch on the torch, and ask: 'What do you see? Is the picture upside down? Is it still the same shape?' Remind learners not to look into the torch.
records.new: For the pinhole demonstration, stand to the side, dim the room, and ask: 'What do you see on the sheet? Is the picture upside down? Is it still the same shape? What happens to its size when I move the sheet away?' Expected: the picture is upside down, the shape is the same, and it gets bigger as the sheet moves away. Remind learners not to look into the torch.
records.why: Matches the corrected demonstration and adds the expected answers for the teacher.
records.reference: Eugene Hecht, Optics (Pearson), section on the pinhole camera

records.old: what would happen to the angle at A'?'
records.new: what would happen to the angle at B'? Expected answer: the right angle at A stays 90° because its sides are horizontal and vertical, but the angle at B grows from about 26.6° (tan 26.6° = 1/2) to about 36.9° (tan 36.9° = 3/4), so the shape changes.'
records.why: The question asked about the angle at A', but A is the right angle with a horizontal and a vertical side, so stretching x by 2 and y by 3 leaves it at 90°. The expected 'shape changes' answer is only true at B or C. With x by 2 and y by 3, A(1,1), B(3,1), C(1,2) become (2,3), (6,3), (2,6), so A'B' = 4 and A'C' = 3. Checked with a calculator: arctan(1/2) = 26.57° and arctan(3/4) = 36.87°.
records.reference: Euclid's Elements Book VI, Definition 1 (similar rectilinear figures have equal angles and proportional sides)

records.value: In groups of four with a ruler, protractor, pencil and the four print cut-outs (face triangle marked with eye-gap line and chin point), learners complete a data table. To fit 40 minutes, each pair in the group takes half the tasks (one pair Tasks A and B, the other pair Tasks C and D) and the group pools the table; with a double period every pair can do all four tasks. Task A: measure one corner angle of each print (expect 90°; every corner of a rectangle is a right angle). Task B: measure width and height of each print and compute width : height (7 : 9 for original, passport and poster; 1 : 1 for the distorted print). Task C: measure the eye gap along the top and the chin distance down from the eye line (original 5.6 and 7.2; passport 1.4 and 1.8; poster 28 and 36; distorted 1.8 and 1.8) and compute eye gap : chin distance. Task D: measure the apex angle at the chin with a protractor (about 42.5° for the original, passport and poster; about 53° for the distorted print). Each group records results, allowing small measurement error of about 1° or 1 mm, and marks which measurements matched across prints. Support: learners with low vision or fine-motor difficulty can be the reader or recorder, or use enlarged prints with thick lines; any learner may show the same understanding by explaining orally or with a labelled sketch.
records.why: Task A alone asked for 16 angle readings (four corners on each of four prints) before Tasks B, C and D, which cannot be done in about 12 minutes. Splitting the tasks between pairs and reading one corner per print keeps the same evidence. The added support line gives learners with low vision or fine-motor difficulty a role and another way to show understanding (guideline 12).

records.value: Part A (outdoors, about 8 minutes including walking): In groups of four, learners go to a marked area in the school compound. One learner stands upright while the others measure the learner's height and shadow length with a tape measure or ruler and record them. Where possible they also measure the shadow of a tall object such as a flagpole, goalpost or the Nyalenda tree, at the same time. Part B (in class, about 5 minutes): Each group draws the two triangles from the data on grid paper using scale 1 cm : 1 m (so the 12 m shadow is 12 cm and the drawing fits on one sheet): Wanjiru's triangle (vertical side 1.5 cm, base 2 cm, right angle at the ground) and the tree's triangle (base 12 cm, vertical side to be found). They draw the line from the top of the object to the end of the shadow, measure the angle at the end of each shadow with a protractor and record both angles in a table with the height : shadow ratio. If they do not go outside, they use the given data: Wanjiru 1.5 m with 2 m shadow, tree with 12 m shadow, and draw Wanjiru's triangle to scale and the tree's triangle with the vertical side extended until the sun's ray reaches the end of the shadow.
records.why: Observe listed 12 + 10 = 22 minutes, more than half the lesson, before Explain (six steps), the Driving Question Board and Model Building. Now 8 + 5. The drawing scale 1 cm : 0.5 m also needed a 24 cm by 18 cm sheet for the tree triangle (12 m / 0.5 = 24 cm; 9 m / 0.5 = 18 cm), which does not fit an exercise book or A4 portrait; 1 cm : 1 m gives 12 cm by 9 cm.

records.new: Step 6 (if time allows, otherwise homework): In pairs they apply the method

records.value: Groups of 4 receive grid paper (1 cm squares), a ruler, scissors and a worksheet. Part A (about 8 minutes): Each group draws a rectangle of 2 cm × 3 cm on grid paper and counts its area in unit squares (6). They then draw an enlargement with k = 2 (4 cm × 6 cm) and another with k = 3 (6 cm × 9 cm) and count the grid squares (rows × squares per row). If a double period is available, groups also cut the rectangles out and tile them with unit squares. They fill a table: k, new width, new height, area, area ÷ 6. Results: k = 2 gives area 24 and factor 4; k = 3 gives area 54 and factor 9. They also see on their 4 × 6 drawing that halving both sides (k = 1/2, back to 2 × 3) leaves 1/4 of the squares. Part B (about 6 minutes): Learners use the prints data: original 14 × 18 = 252 cm²; passport 3.5 × 4.5 = 15.75 cm²; poster 70 × 90 = 6300 cm². Each pair of learners takes one pair of prints (then the group shares the rows) and calculates the linear scale factor k and the area factor (area of image ÷ area of object): original to passport k = 1/4, area factor 15.75 ÷ 252 = 1/16; original to poster k = 5, area factor 6300 ÷ 252 = 25; passport to poster k = 20, area factor 6300 ÷ 15.75 = 400. They add these rows to their table and compare area factor with k.
records.why: Observe listed 12 + 10 = 22 minutes, with cutting out and tiling several rectangles. Counting squares on a drawing gives the same data (areas 24 and 54, factors 4 and 9) in 8 minutes; cutting and tiling stays as the double-period option the lesson title already allows. Part B is split between pairs.

records.new: Give 2 minutes for writing, then

records.new: three 5-minute stations
records.why: Three 6-minute stations is 18 minutes before moving between tables; with Predict, Explain, the Driving Question Board and Model Building the lesson overran 40 minutes. Station C repeats Lesson 7 and can be short.

records.new: Give a time call at the 5-minute mark

records.old: In the Explain phase, groups write a claim-evidence-reasoning Final Explanation and test it against a new challenge.
records.new: In the Explain phase, groups write a claim-evidence-reasoning Final Explanation and test it against a new challenge. Timing plan for 40 minutes: Predict 4, Evidence Table 8 (copy the values from the earlier lessons and measure only two cells), Explain 12 (the Transfer Challenge becomes the exit task if time runs out), Driving Question Board 6, Model Building 10; a double period is better if available.
records.why: Five full phases (evidence table, Final Explanation with transfer task, resolving the whole board, final model and comparison) do not fit 40 minutes without a plan. Budget adds to 4 + 8 + 12 + 6 + 10 = 40.

records.old: (Both should be close to 37°, since tan 37° ≈ 0.75, but learners just compare them.)
records.new: (With the given data, tan 37° ≈ 0.75 = 1.5 ÷ 2, so both angles should be close to 37°. With learners' own outdoor data the angle depends on the time of day: near the equator shadows are very short around midday, so measure in the morning or late afternoon. Learners only compare the two angles, which should agree.)
records.why: The 37° value is only true for the given data (shadow 2 m for a 1.5 m object). Learners' real outdoor shadows in Kisumu (about 0 degrees latitude) can be almost zero near noon, so a teacher expecting 37° outdoors would think the measurement failed. Checked: arctan(1.5/2) = 36.87°.
records.reference: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Solar Calculator (solar elevation by latitude and time of day)

records.old: Intervene if a group sorts by size alone.
records.new: Teacher key: similar to the original are the passport and poster prints, the Kenya map and its smaller copy, the two same-shaped school logos, the matatu model and the matatu picture (only if the model is a true scale model with wheels and windows in proportion), and a pair of triangles prepared with equal angles (for example 3-4-5 cm and 6-8-10 cm). Not similar: the 4.5 × 4.5 cm print and the squashed logo. Intervene if a group sorts by size alone.
records.why: Teachers were told to prepare 'a pair of triangles' and a matatu pair but not which pairs are similar, so they could not judge the groups' sorting. 3-4-5 and 6-8-10 are similar with k = 2 (6/3 = 8/4 = 10/5 = 2).

records.old: using learners' own words.
records.new: using learners' own words. Kiswahili support (suggested terms, teachers to confirm): maumbo yanayofanana (similar figures), ukuzaji (enlargement), upunguzaji (reduction), uwiano (ratio), kigezo cha ukuzaji (scale factor). Write them beside the English terms and let learners use either language in group talk.
records.why: The sequence had no Kiswahili or other language supports for English learners. These terms are my suggestion and I could not verify them against the Kenyan mathematics Kiswahili glossary; teachers must confirm or correct the terms before use.

records.new: Finally, learners sketch an initial model of their current thinking, which will be revised through Lesson 12. Preparation (no printer needed): before the lesson draw the four prints on paper as rectangles at the sizes given (the 70 × 90 cm poster as a taped outline on the wall or floor), each with the same simple face sketch, an oval face with an eye line and a chin point that form a face triangle. The face triangle measures 5.6 cm and 7.2 cm (eye gap and chin distance) on the original, 1.4 and 1.8 on the passport print, 28 and 36 on the poster and 1.8 and 1.8 on the distorted print; these numbers are used from Lesson 3.
records.why: Lessons 1 to 3 depend on 'prepared prints' with a face triangle of exact sizes, but nothing told the teacher how to make them with school resources. Sizes match Lesson 3: 5.6 : 7.2 = 1.4 : 1.8 = 28 : 36 = 7 : 9, and 1.8 : 1.8 for the distorted print.

records.new: Preview Lesson 8: 'Next we shall construct enlargements from a centre using rays.' KICD project (optional, out of class over Lessons 7 to 11): groups use locally available materials such as card, boxes or clay to make a pair of similar solids (cubes or cuboids and, if possible, cylinders) of different sizes, record k, the area factor and the volume factor, and show them in a class display.
records.why: The KICD suggested learning experiences end with a project: make sets of models of solids (cubes, cuboids, cylinders, spheres) of different sizes using similarity and enlargement from locally available materials. Nothing in the 12 lessons covered it, although the KICD competency 'Creativity and Imagination' depends on it. Teachers decide whether to run it and with which solids.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.1 Similarity and Enlargement

records.old: The trial print fails both tests, so its shape changed.
records.new: The trial print still has 90° corners, but it fails the ratio test (1 : 1, not 7 : 9) and the chin-angle test (about 53°, not about 42.5°), so its shape changed. Equal corner angles alone are not enough.
records.why: The exemplar said the trial print fails both tests, but its corners are still 90°, which Lesson 3 explicitly teaches. The exemplar now says exactly which checks it passes and fails, so it matches Lesson 3 and the rest of this exemplar (all corners 90°).

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: States a clear claim, supports it with exact data (7:9 vs 1:1, about 42.5° vs about 53°, k = 1/4 and 5 vs 9/28 and 1/4) and links the evidence to the idea of similarity.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: States a correct claim and uses some correct data, but the reasoning linking the data to similarity is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Claim is unclear or missing, or uses little or incorrect evidence.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Calculates every k as image ÷ object, names the object and the image, and correctly identifies enlargement or reduction. Compares the unequal factors of the trial print.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Calculates most scale factors correctly but sometimes omits the object and image or the enlargement/reduction label.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Calculations are mostly incorrect or the object and image are mixed up.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly uses k² and k³ with Wanjiru's prints and the cartons, and explains why doubling lengths does not double the area.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses k² and k³ correctly in most cases but explanations are brief.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Treats area or volume as changing by k, or makes errors in the calculations.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Finds images and the centre correctly, solves the map, sign cost and shadow problems accurately, and uses ~, corresponding sides and corresponding angles, units and width-first order correctly.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Solves most application problems correctly with minor errors in units, notation or the order of width and height.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Has many errors in the applications, or little correct use of terms and units.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives a complete explanation that size can change but shape is kept only if one scale factor is applied to all lengths. Connects to the key inquiry question (how similarity and enlargement are applied in day-to-day life) with real examples.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives a correct answer to the driving question but with limited links to everyday examples.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Answer is incomplete or does not explain why the trial print is distorted.

records.why: The contract has three level fields, so the CBE level names are written into the descriptor text: Exceeds, Meets and Approaches Expectations. Descriptor wording is unchanged otherwise, except that criterion 5 now names the single KICD key inquiry question.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the current data contract and printed headings allow only three. Below Expectations cannot be represented; the 'developing' field is used for Approaches. Teachers or the partner may wish to extend the contract.

The learner is called 'Wanjiru Atieno' and lives in Kisumu. Wanjiru is a typical Kikuyu given name and Atieno a Luo one, so the pairing is unusual for a Kisumu schoolgirl. 'Wanjiru' is also in lesson titles, which I may not change. Suggested: keep or change the name across the sequence (for example a single-community name such as 'Akinyi Atieno'); this needs a decision for all 12 lessons and the Final Explanation.

The painting cost of KES 400 per square metre is an assumed price. Teachers should replace it with a typical local sign-writing rate if known; the rate appears in the Lesson 11 text, summary table and Final Explanation Section 5(d), and the answers (KES 252, KES 2268, KES 1008) would change with it.

The aresKeywords of Lessons 1 and 2 include 'scale factor', 'ratio', 'corresponding sides' and 'corresponding angles'. A matched video or slide on those terms would give away the discovery before Lesson 3 and 4. Suggest removing those words from Lesson 1 and 2 keywords or checking the resources the matcher picks for them.

KICD content not (fully) taught: (1) area and volume scale factors are taught only for rectangles and cuboids, while outcome (c) says 'different figures and solids' (a Lesson 8 triangle ABC has area 1 and its k = 2 image area 4, which would be an easy extension); (2) the project with cylinders and spheres (see Lesson 7 record); (3) the KICD experience 'use digital devices' is not used because lessons assume no electricity. Number and name check: KICD Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.1 Similarity and Enlargement, 12 lessons - matches the data, no mismatch.
